body:
Animal Husbandry in Harappan Society

Agriculture was closely associated with animal husbandry, or the rearing and management of domesticated animals. Livestock supplied food and other resources and could also provide labour for agricultural and transport activities.

Animal remains recovered from Harappan settlements include the bones of cattle, sheep, goats, buffaloes and pigs. These animals formed part of the domesticated livestock economy.

AnimalStatus or evidencePrincipal significance
CattleDomesticated; represented in figurines and sealsFood resources and probable draught power
Sheep and goatsDomesticated livestockMeat and other animal products
BuffaloesDomesticated animalsAnimal products and potential working animals
PigsDomestic pig remains identifiedSource of meat
Fish and wild animalsRemains found at settlementsAdditional food obtained through fishing, hunting or other means

Why Cattle Were Important

Cattle had several possible uses. They could provide milk and other animal products, while oxen were suitable for pulling agricultural implements and carts.

Representations of humped bulls are particularly familiar from Harappan material culture. However, an animal depicted on a seal should not automatically be interpreted as evidence for every possible economic or religious use of that animal.

Pastoral Movement and Grazing

Pastoralism refers to a livelihood substantially based on maintaining herds of domesticated animals.

Pastures and water sources were available around many Harappan settlements. During dry months, however, large herds may have needed to move to more distant areas in search of grazing land and water.

Such seasonal movement would have helped communities make use of pastures beyond their immediate settlements. It does not mean that all Harappan herders were permanently nomadic. Animal husbandry could be practised alongside settled agriculture.

Wild Animals and Hunting

Remains of wild animals, including deer, wild boar and gharial, have been identified at Harappan sites. The discovery of wild animal bones shows that people had access to resources from the surrounding environment.

However, the presence of such bones does not always establish that the inhabitants of the settlement personally hunted the animals. Meat and other animal products could also have been obtained from groups engaged in hunting.

The distinction between domesticated animals and wild species is important when reconstructing Harappan food systems.

Fishing and Other Food Resources

The Harappans ate fish, as demonstrated by fish remains recovered from settlements. Fishing was possible in rivers, streams and coastal waters.

Coastal settlements in Gujarat and Sind were particularly well positioned to obtain marine resources. Fishing therefore complemented agricultural and pastoral activities.

Other food resources included wild fruits, such as ber or jujube. These could be collected from the surrounding countryside.

The Harappan diet was therefore not restricted to cultivated grains. It included a combination of plant foods, domesticated animal products, fish and some wild resources.

Preparing and Cooking Food

Harvested grain generally requires processing before consumption. The Harappans used stone grinding implements, pottery vessels and other domestic equipment for this purpose.

Grinding Grain with Querns

Querns were stone implements used for grinding or crushing grain and other materials. Saddle querns discovered at Mohenjodaro show that grain processing was an established household activity.

A saddle quern generally consisted of a larger grinding stone over which a smaller stone was moved. Repeated rubbing or crushing could break grain into smaller particles or flour.

Cooking and Storage Vessels

Pottery vessels served different domestic purposes, including cooking, carrying water, keeping food and storing agricultural products.

Large jars could hold grain and other provisions. Smaller pots and bowls were useful for preparing, serving and consuming food.

Investigations of residues preserved in some Harappan pottery have also reported dairy products and traces associated with plant foods such as turmeric, ginger and banana. These findings indicate dietary variety, but individual reports should not be treated as proof that all such foods were staple crops throughout the civilisation.

Food Storage and Urban Supply

Food storage was essential in an economy where crops were harvested seasonally but consumed throughout the year. Grain also needed to be retained for future sowing.

Storage could occur in households, settlements and larger facilities. Large jars, storage spaces and substantial buildings provide information about the handling of goods and provisions.

Granaries and Warehouses

Several substantial Harappan buildings have traditionally been described as granaries or warehouses.

At Harappa, a large building on Mound F was historically identified as a granary. However, the identification is not certain because the excavated structure did not provide clear concentrations of stored grain or storage containers. Its function remains debated.

At Mohenjodaro, a substantial building on the Citadel has also been described as a warehouse. The surviving structure indicates substantial construction, but the precise goods stored there are not established.

At Lothal in Gujarat, a structure interpreted as a storehouse was associated with seals and sealings. These finds suggest that goods were stored or handled in an organised manner.

Storage buildings and historical certainty

It is reasonable to conclude that Harappan communities stored food and other goods. It is not equally certain that every large building traditionally called a granary was used specifically for storing grain.

The Relationship Between Food and Craft Production

Urban occupations depended upon the wider food-producing economy. A bead-maker or metalworker spending substantial time on specialised production could not simultaneously devote the same time to cultivating food.

Reliable agricultural and pastoral production therefore helped support the division of labour characteristic of Harappan settlements.

Prelims focus

  • Domesticated animals included cattle, sheep, goats, buffaloes and pigs.
  • Wild animal remains include deer, boar and gharial.
  • Fish formed part of the Harappan diet.
  • Stone querns were used for grinding grain and other materials.
  • Lothal had a storehouse associated with seals and sealings.
  • Trap: The traditional identification of the large Harappa structure as a granary is not archaeologically conclusive.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 2–4 and 8; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 38–40; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 96–97; Jonathan Mark Kenoyer, Granary, Harappa, Around the Indus in 90 Slides, Harappa.com, accessed 17 November 2026.]

title: Animal Husbandry, Fishing, Food Preparation and Storage

body:
Development of Metalworking

The Harappan civilisation possessed considerable skill in producing metal objects. Its craftspeople made tools, weapons, vessels, ornaments and figurines from different metals and alloys.

The civilisation is commonly described as belonging to the Bronze Age because copper and bronze were important technological materials. However, Harappan people continued to use stone tools as well. The use of bronze did not mean that every tool was metallic.

Metallurgy

Metallurgy is the knowledge and practice of obtaining, processing and working metals to produce useful objects. Activities may include melting, casting, hammering, shaping and joining metal.

Metals Used by the Harappans

Metal or alloyPropertiesHarappan uses
CopperRelatively soft and workableTools, vessels, mirrors, ornaments and other implements
BronzeA copper-based alloy, generally harder than pure copper when appropriately preparedTools, vessels and cast figurines
GoldValuable and easily shapedBeads, ornaments and jewellery
SilverWorkable precious metalOrnaments and vessels

Copper and Bronze

Bronze is an alloy, meaning a metallic material made by combining metals or a metal with another element. The standard textbook example is an alloy of copper and tin. Some ancient copper-based alloys also contained arsenic.

Bronze could be harder than pure copper and was useful for making tools and other objects. Copper and bronze implements found at Harappan sites include chisels, knives, axes, blades, needles and other working tools.

Copper is a metal. Bronze is an alloy, commonly made from copper and tin. They should not be treated as identical materials.

Gold and Silver

Gold and silver were mainly valued for ornaments and some special vessels. Jewellery included beads, rings, bracelets and other decorative objects.

The use of both base metals and precious metals shows that Harappan metalworking served everyday practical requirements as well as ornament production.

Metalworking Techniques

Metalworkers could shape objects in several ways. These included hammering metal into a desired form, preparing thin sheets, cutting pieces, and pouring molten metal into moulds.

Casting involves pouring molten metal into a prepared mould and allowing it to cool and solidify. The object takes the shape of the space inside the mould.

One especially important technique associated with Harappan bronze sculpture was lost-wax casting.

The Lost-Wax or Cire Perdue Technique

The lost-wax technique, also called cire perdue, allows a metal object to be produced from a model originally made of wax.

The wax is removed before molten metal is introduced into the mould. The metal then occupies the space previously filled by the wax.

Main Steps in Lost-Wax Casting

  1. Prepare a wax model: The craftsperson makes the desired figure or object in wax.
  2. Apply a clay covering: The wax figure is covered with clay to form a mould. Suitable openings are left for removing the wax and introducing molten metal.
  3. Dry and heat the mould: Heating melts the wax, which flows out through the openings.
  4. Form the hollow space: Removal of the wax leaves a cavity corresponding to the original model.
  5. Pour molten metal: Molten bronze or another suitable metal is introduced into the cavity.
  6. Cool and remove the mould: After the metal solidifies, the clay covering is broken away to reveal the cast object.

The technique allowed craftspeople to reproduce detailed and complicated forms. The original wax model was destroyed during casting, which distinguishes the process from methods that repeatedly use an unchanged rigid mould.

The Bronze Dancing Girl of Mohenjodaro

The famous bronze figure popularly called the Dancing Girl was discovered at Mohenjodaro. It is an important example of Harappan skill in metal casting.

The figure shows a standing young female with distinctive ornaments and a confident posture. Its small size and carefully shaped form demonstrate the ability of Harappan craftspeople to produce detailed metal sculptures.

The title Dancing Girl is a conventional modern name. It should not be interpreted as proof that the individual represented was actually a dancer.

Other Examples of Metal Figures

Bronze and copper figures of animals have also been discovered at Harappan sites.

  • Lothal, Gujarat: copper figures of a dog and a bird.
  • Kalibangan, Rajasthan: a bronze figure of a bull.
  • Mohenjodaro: the bronze figure known as the Dancing Girl.

Such discoveries show that metal casting was not restricted to a single settlement.

Sources of Metals

Harappan settlements required supplies of copper, tin and precious metals. Some raw materials were obtained through contacts with regions beyond the major urban settlements.

The Khetri region of Rajasthan was an important potential source of copper. Copper may also have been obtained from Oman. Tin may have come from regions corresponding to present-day Afghanistan and Iran, while gold may have been obtained from southern India, including the Karnataka region.

These source identifications vary in their degree of certainty. They demonstrate the importance of connections between raw-material regions and Harappan craft centres, but do not establish a single source for every metal object.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan metalworking prominently used copper and bronze.
  • Bronze is commonly an alloy of copper and tin.
  • Lost-wax casting is also called cire perdue.
  • The Dancing Girl is a bronze figure from Mohenjodaro.
  • Lothal yielded copper animal figures; Kalibangan yielded a bronze bull figure.
  • Trap: Bronze Age does not mean that the Harappans stopped using stone tools or commonly used iron tools.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 9–11, section Bronze Casting; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 36–38; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 97–98; V. N. Prabhakar, Protohistory of India and Pakistan III: Indus Crafts and Arts, INFLIBNET, section 2.10, Metallurgy, accessed 17 November 2026.]
